name: TCA CROSS

lead: TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars) is a dermatology procedure in which a clinician applies a high concentration of trichloroacetic acid to the base of individual atrophic acne scars, most often narrow icepick scars, rather than peeling the whole face. The payoff is shallower scars and smoother-looking skin.

The acid causes a controlled injury in the dermis, which authors propose triggers new collagen formation and lifts the scar floor. Published studies, mostly small and many without a control group, report meaningful improvement after a series of sessions, including in darker skin types. Comparisons against subcision, microneedling and pinpoint CO2 laser have been mixed.

paras: A clinician dabs the acid into each scar and repeats sessions every few weeks, with studies using concentrations from 50% to 100%. It is often combined with other scar treatments. Improvement is judged over the weeks and months after a series.

The original authors reported no significant complications in a 65-patient series. Acid at these strengths is not an over-the-counter product and the procedure is clinician-performed. Trials are small and mostly open-label.

chain: Skin rebuilds collagen in the pit
angle.text: TCA CROSS is used by dermatologists to make narrow, deep icepick acne scars shallower by applying strong acid to individual scars, prompting collagen to rebuild in the pit. Small trials report improvement, including in darker skin types.

lead: TCA CROSS, short for chemical reconstruction of skin scars, is a dermatologic technique for atrophic (depressed) acne scars in which a clinician applies a high-concentration trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution to individual scars rather than to the whole face. It was described by Korean authors in a 2002 report on patients with dark skin types [1]. For people with icepick scars, the narrow pitted marks that stay visible after acne clears, it is one of the focal options for raising the scar floor and smoothing the skin's texture.

Acne scarring is common: Wikipedia cites estimates that scars affect about 95 percent of people with acne, and that atrophic scars make up roughly 75 percent of acne scars.[2] Because icepick scars are narrow, under about 2 mm across, and extend into the dermis, people searching for ways to smooth skin texture often look for procedures that treat them one at a time, which is where TCA CROSS enters the conversation.[2][1]

It is most associated with icepick scars and deep, narrow boxcar scars, which are described in dermatology literature as hard to improve with whole-face resurfacing [2]. Published studies use concentrations from 50% to 100% and typically repeat sessions every few weeks [1][3][4][5].

The evidence consists mostly of small prospective or retrospective series, with a few randomised comparisons against other scar treatments. A 2017 systematic review examined the efficacy and adverse reactions of non-energy-based acne scar treatments [6]. Review authors have noted that few randomised trials exist to identify any single gold-standard approach to acne scarring.

A 2026 review of 34 publications covering 937 patients, mostly for icepick and boxcar acne scars, reported improvement rates of 50 to 80 percent, high satisfaction, and transient post-inflammatory pigment change as the most common adverse event; it found that multiple sessions gave greater improvement and higher concentrations raised complication risk, and it called for more standardised techniques [7].

paras: Acne scars are commonly classified as icepick, boxcar and rolling types, a classification proposed in a 2001 review that also set out a treatment algorithm including punch techniques, subcision and laser resurfacing. Icepick scars are narrow (generally under 2 mm) and extend into the dermis [2].

In TCA CROSS, as described in the original report, the acid is applied by pressing on the depressed area of the scar rather than spreading it across the skin, so the surrounding tissue is largely spared [1]. Procedural details such as applicator choice, number of passes and aftercare vary between clinicians and are not covered here.

The technique was named in a 2002 Dermatologic Surgery report by Korean authors, who described pressing higher-strength TCA onto the depressed area of atrophic acne scars in patients with darker skin types and called the method chemical reconstruction of skin scars, or CROSS.[1] Earlier practice, as the 2008 follow-up describes it, used strengths around 90 percent, and later authors tested lower strengths including 50 percent and 70 percent to lower the risk of side effects.[4][5]

In 2006, a histologic study of three patients treated with serial focal 95 percent TCA applied with wooden applicators every six weeks for six treatments reported reduced scar depth, more collagen fibres and fragmented elastic fibres in biopsies taken a year later, with high patient satisfaction and no complications.[8] By the 2010s the technique appeared in standard acne-scar reviews alongside subcision, microneedling, fillers and lasers; the 2017 systematic review of non-energy-based treatments, for example, covered 36 articles across subcision, dermabrasion, microneedling, dermal fillers and chemical peeling.[6] A 2019 dermatology-clinics review lists chemical peels and subcision among the least invasive scar-revision modalities.[9]

sections.h: Where it fits among scar treatments
paras: Dermatology reviews describe acne scarring as usually needing more than one tool, because icepick, boxcar and rolling scars respond differently: subcision releases the fibrous bands under rolling scars, microneedling and fractional lasers work across areas of skin, fillers lift depressions, and focal methods such as punch techniques, pinpoint laser and CROSS aim at individual narrow scars.[6][2] Wikipedia notes that lasers and light therapies are generally an add-on rather than first-line options because of cost and limited evidence.[2]

Published comparisons treat CROSS as one arm among several: against microneedling in a 30-participant randomised study, against subcision in a split-face study of rolling scars, and against pinpoint CO2 laser in a randomised pilot of icepick scars.[3][10][11] A registered trial pairing subcision with either diluted calcium hydroxylapatite or CROSS has been completed.[12] Because most trials are small, reviews tend to describe the evidence in terms of ranges rather than a single standard.[7]

sections.h: How it is thought to work
paras: The original authors proposed that the focal high-strength acid injures the scar tissue in a controlled way, prompting new collagen deposition that raises the base of the scar [1]. A later comparative study describes the method's advantage as reconstructing scars by increasing dermal thickening and collagen production [3]. Histology in one small series examined samples from two patients' back scars [4].

The 2002 series compared 65% and 100% TCA [1]. A 2008 report examined 50% TCA, as opposed to the roughly 90% used in earlier work, with the stated aim of reducing local adverse effects [4]. A 2015 study evaluated 70% TCA in 53 patients [5].

sections.h: Scar types and why they are hard to treat
paras: Acne scars are commonly sorted into icepick, boxcar and rolling types, a classification set out in a 2001 review. Icepick scars are narrow and extend into the dermis, which is why whole-face resurfacing is described as having limited effect on them and why focal approaches such as CROSS, punch techniques, pinpoint laser and subcision are used.[2] Dermatology reviews describe atrophic scars as having a significant psychosocial impact on quality of life.[7]

In the 2002 case series of 65 patients with Fitzpatrick skin types IV-V, 82% of the 65% TCA group and 94% of the 100% TCA group were reported to have a good clinical response, and the authors reported no significant complications [1].
A randomised study of 30 participants compared four sessions of percutaneous collagen induction (microneedling) with four sessions of 100% TCA CROSS and reported improvement in both groups [3].

A split-face comparison in 20 patients with rolling scars (skin types III-IV) found that subcision produced significantly greater reduction in scar size and depth than 100% TCA CROSS, with fewer side effects, although scar depth continued to decrease over time after CROSS [10].
A 2014 randomised pilot study of 28 patients with icepick scars compared pinpoint CO2 laser irradiation with TCA CROSS and reported greater improvement with the laser [11].

In a 2015 study of 53 patients, 66% had good or excellent improvement (over 50%) on physician and patient assessments after 70% TCA CROSS, and 81.1% were satisfied or very satisfied; outcomes were better in patients with predominantly boxcar scars and higher baseline severity [5].

A five-patient report of 50% TCA described improvement in depth and appearance of scars on the face and back [4]. A registered trial comparing subcision followed by diluted calcium hydroxylapatite injection with subcision followed by TCA CROSS has been completed with 13 participants; no results are listed in the registry entry [12].

A 2025 randomised trial of 40 patients compared 70% and 100% TCA used in the CROSS technique and found no significant difference in overall efficacy between them; crusting lasted longer with 100%, and within the 100% group icepick scars responded significantly better than boxcar scars.[13]

A 2022 blinded split-face trial in 45 patients tested topical 0.5% timolol and saline injection as additions to TCA CROSS. CROSS improved scars on all sides; timolol sides showed a significant reduction in the severity and duration of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and higher satisfaction, while saline injected before CROSS did not reduce scar numbers, and no permanent complications were seen.[14]

The 2026 review described above pooled 20 clinical trials, 4 comparative or cohort studies, 4 case series, 2 case reports and 4 expert opinions, with patients aged 4 to 65 and Fitzpatrick types I to V; CROSS was also used on varicella and leishmaniasis scars, and fine-gauge needles and paintbrushes were described as giving more precise delivery.[7]

The original 2002 report stated there were no significant complications [1], and a 2015 study concluded 70% TCA was safe in all atrophic scar types [5]. The subcision comparison reported more side effects with 100% TCA CROSS than with subcision [10]. Pigmentation change is a commonly discussed concern with chemical peeling in general; the original series was conducted in patients with Fitzpatrick skin types IV-V [1]. Because studies differ in how they record adverse events and are small, rates are not firmly established.

The 2026 review reported transient post-inflammatory pigmentary change as the most common adverse event and found higher TCA concentrations increased complication risk.[7] In the 70% versus 100% comparison, crusting was longer at 100%.[13] In a pigmentation-focused split-face trial, topical timolol shortened the duration of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after CROSS.[14] TCA at these strengths is a clinician-applied agent; studies were mostly small and open-label.

TCA is a corrosive chemical: its safety classification carries a danger signal word for severe skin and eye damage, and Wikipedia lists its use in chemical peels, tattoo removal and wart treatment.[15] In July 2024 the US Food and Drug Administration warned consumers against buying or using chemical peel products sold for home use without professional supervision. The agency said it has approved no chemical peel products, that products containing TCA, glycolic, salicylic and lactic acids were sold at strengths too high for home use, and that injuries could include severe burns, pain, swelling, infection, skin colour changes and disfiguring scars, some requiring emergency or specialist care.[16] Its warning letters named products including 100 percent and 50 percent TCA peels.[16]

The agency said depth of penetration depends on concentration, number of applications and how long the product stays on the skin, and recommended that chemical peels be considered only under a dermatologist or other licensed, trained practitioner.[16] The 2026 review reports that higher concentrations raised complication risk and that post-inflammatory pigment change was the most common adverse event.[7]

TCA CROSS is categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx, the community's term for procedural interventions, and it features in appearance discussion as a focal option for icepick scars, usually alongside subcision, microneedling, fractional lasers and fillers.[3][10][11][7] Wikipedia describes the wider looksmaxxing scene as starting in 2010s forums and reaching TikTok in the early 2020s, with skincare and grooming grouped under 'softmaxxing' and procedures under 'hardmaxxing'.[17]
Home-peel products with very high acid strengths are the aspect that regulators have commented on publicly, as described in the safety section above.[16]
